To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

teachers believe that they should be involved in testing, that they believe that they should have more information about testing than they now have, and that they do not have the information that they believe they should have.
teachers are confident in tests but not in test interpretation, and that teachers are willing to share test scores with pupils and parents but are reluctant to do so.

teachers believe that test scores have great value, that they use test scores in many ways, and that their use of test scores has increased greatly in recent years. (p. 3) The third theme is that of the teacher's role in testing.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of a program to improve the quality of the teacher.
the development of a new approach to the problem of the "true" problem.

the measurement of the attitudes of teachers toward testing and the use of test scores in the classroom, and with the relationships among teachers' attitudes toward testing, their use of test scores, their knowledge of measurement, and their professional training.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the teacher's attitudes and beliefs about tests are generally positive and that he feels a need for more information about tests and their use.
the teachers in this study have an attitude toward testing which is generally favorable and which is consistent in its major aspects.
teachers believe in tests and use them a great deal, but that they have not been prepared to understand the nature and the limitations of tests and the ways in which they can be used.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
teachers believe that testing is a good thing and that they are doing a good job of it.
the teacher is a person who is not well informed about the nature of testing and its uses, and that the teacher is not well prepared to deal with the problems of testing.
teachers are not very well prepared to use tests, but that they do use them, and they use them with great confidence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no single best way of measuring attitudes, but rather a number of different approaches that can be used depending on the specific situation and the purpose of the research.
the data provide evidence that teachers are not as opposed to the use of tests as is sometimes supposed and that they are not as ignorant of measurement theory and practice as is sometimes assumed.
there is no single, universal, best way to measure a student's progress, or even a single, universal, "best" test.
